name: Emeka Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm head shepherd on the Carrick Hill estate, about fourteen hundred ewes spread over the high ground. Most days I'm on the quad by six with Bess and Moss, my two collies, checking the hill before the weather turns. Lambing's the hard bit, three weeks of maybe four hours' sleep a night. I also run ninety ewes of my own on some rented ground below the road, which is my bit of savings walking about on four legs.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being up there when it's quiet and the dogs are working well, it's the best feeling there is. What wears me out is the paperwork and the estate office ringing about numbers. Davey, the old stockman I eat my sandwiches with, says the hill hasn't changed, only the people in the office have. I mostly agree with him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. Good, honestly. That's what I'd like to hear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, to be fair. In the pub on Mill Street I'd say the computer people promised the moon and gave us a better spreadsheet. Online I don't post much, but I might share something about it being a bubble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved, because a computer was never going to gather sheep off a wet hill in fog. What would still bother me is that the estate office might use the bits that do work to squeeze us on hours. Small tools in the wrong hands still cost the lads money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, plain and simple. Keep building my own flock, maybe up to a hundred and twenty ewes by next autumn if the rented ground stays mine. If the office brings in some new app for the lambing records, I'd let the young lad fill it in and keep my notebook in my top pocket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels steady. Like a normal year, which is all I want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the office might use the tools to squeeze hours. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd count every minute on the quad from some tracker and decide the gathers take too long. Last year they already tried cutting Davey's overtime at clipping time. A machine that counts minutes doesn't know a ewe is stuck in a gully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever try one of the tools yourself, even a small one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, no. My partner Ruth uses it to plan lessons and she shows me sometimes, but it's not for me. I'd rather ring the vet than ask a phone what's wrong with a ewe.

S0.say: I'd say the computer people promised the moon and gave us a better spreadsheet. Nobody's gathering sheep off a wet hill with an app, and I'd be glad to say I called it.
S0.think: He's relieved, because the hill work stays his. His one private worry is that the estate office would use the small tools to count minutes and cut the workers' hours.
S0.do: Keeps working as head shepherd and grows his own flock from ninety to about a hundred and twenty ewes by next autumn. Leaves any new record-keeping app to the junior and keeps his paper notebook.
S0.feel: Settled and relieved, with a small, familiar suspicion of the estate office.
S0.quote: A machine that counts minutes doesn't know a ewe is stuck in a gully.
S0.fieldNote: Emeka hears the plateau as good news and slips quickly into a story about overtime being cut, which shows where his real fears sit: with bosses, not machines. He has never used AI and sees no reason to start. His savings are mostly sheep, which ties his security to the land he already knows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Strong change but not a revolution. Right. So it does come, just slower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say it's fine for us on the hill, it's the valley farms that'll see the robots first. To friends I'd say the government needs to make sure workers get a share, not just the landowners. That's what I'd post too if I posted anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the estate would buy a drone to count sheep and a fancy collar system, and then decide they need one shepherd instead of three. Davey would go first because he's sixty-one. I'd probably survive, but I'd be doing three men's ground with gadgets I don't trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the farmworkers' union this winter, which I keep meaning to do anyway. I'd put more of my wage into the flock and less into the bank, so I've got my own thing if the estate cuts back. I'd learn the drone if they forced me, but I wouldn't volunteer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared yet, more like hearing a weather warning for next week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the drone only if forced. Why not get ahead of it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because once you're the one who knows the gadget, you're the one they keep and your mate goes. I don't want to be the reason Davey gets his papers. That sounds daft, maybe, but that's how it'd feel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Davey if the estate did cut back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to go to the union before he signs anything. Then I'd probably buy him a pint and say nothing much, because he'd hate a fuss. He's taught me most of what I know about reading a hill.

S1.say: He'd say the hill farms are safer than the valley ones and that workers, not just landowners, have to get a share of what the new tools save. He'd put it to friends and the union the same way.
S1.think: He privately expects the estate to use drones and collars to run the hill with one shepherd instead of three. He thinks he'd survive but that his older workmate Davey would be let go first.
S1.do: Joins the farmworkers' union this winter and puts more of his wage into his own flock as a backup. Learns the estate's drone only if he is told to, not before.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like hearing a weather warning for next week, and protective of his older workmate.
S1.quote: Once you're the one who knows the gadget, you're the one they keep and your mate goes.
S1.fieldNote: His refusal to learn the drone is partly about loyalty, not only dislike of technology, which was a surprise. He frames the risk as a fairness problem between estate and workers. His own flock is quietly becoming his plan B.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? By 2028? That's two lambings from now. That's nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a choice the big companies made for everyone without asking us. I'd be at any meeting going, saying the government has to stop it or tax it hard. I'd probably even post, which I never do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd lose the estate job inside a year, because the owner's son would love robot shepherds. Two years isn't long enough for anyone to retrain into anything, and what would I even retrain into if robots do everything? My ninety ewes would be all I've got, and I'm not sure who'd buy the lambs either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything that isn't the flock or the rent straight away. I'd go to the union and push for a proper redundancy deal before the machines land, not after. If the estate let me go, I'd ask about taking on more rented ground cheap, because I reckon plenty of land would be going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake doing sums, which I never do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years of warning give you, compared with none?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next to nothing, to be honest. It gives me time to get angry and to sign up to things, but not time to become a different person. You can't learn a new trade properly in two winters while you're still lambing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ruth the night you knew it was coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we're all right for money for a while, which is true. Then I'd probably go out and check the ewes in the dark for no reason, just to be doing something. She'd know what that meant.

S2.say: He'd say it's a choice the big companies made without asking anyone, and that the government must stop it or tax it hard. He'd go to every meeting and even post online, which he never does.
S2.think: He believes he'd lose the estate job within a year and that two years is too short to retrain into anything. His own flock would be all he had, and he isn't sure there'd be buyers for the lambs.
S2.do: Cuts all spending except the flock and rent at once and pushes through the union for a proper redundancy deal before the machines arrive. If let go, tries to rent more land cheaply as others leave it.
S2.feel: Alarmed and sleepless, doing sums at night that he never used to do.
S2.quote: It gives me time to get angry and to sign up to things, but not time to become a different person.
S2.fieldNote: Two years of warning gives Emeka time for protest but not for change, and he knows it. His instinct under pressure is to hold on to land and animals rather than try anything new. The moment with Ruth, checking ewes in the dark, said more than his answers about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. 2031. I'd be thirty-two. Still young, which is either good or worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, really: workers need a say in this and the profits need sharing out. I'd be more organised about it with five years, though, less shouting. I'd push the union to make it about rural jobs, not just factories.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I'd see the first robots come on the valley farms and know mine was next. The part that scares me is watching it come and still not changing, because that's me, I don't change easy. I might just stand there with the dogs until it's done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first couple of years putting money into my own ground, maybe trying to buy a small hill block instead of renting. I'd go to the union branch every month and get onto the committee. I'd probably let Ruth talk me into a course of some kind, something like fencing contracting or dry stone walling, the stuff the posh houses will still want done by hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a bit of fight in it. Like a long gather where you can see the storm over the next hill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might just stand there until it's done. What would stop that happening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth, mostly. She'd sit me down at the kitchen table with a list, she does that. And Davey would tell me not to be a fool, he's watched lads like me wait too long before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why dry stone walling? Why do you think that would last?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because people with money pay for things that look old and made by hand. There's a walling job at the big house near the reservoir that's three years waiting for a man. A robot could probably do it, but I'd bet some folk would rather pay for me.

S3.say: He'd repeat that workers need a say and the profits need sharing, but with five years he'd be more organised and push the union to fight for rural jobs, not just factory ones.
S3.think: He fears watching the robots arrive on the valley farms and still not changing, because he knows he doesn't change easily. He worries he'd stand there with the dogs until it's over.
S3.do: Puts money towards buying a small hill block instead of renting, and joins the local union committee. Lets his partner talk him into a hand-craft course such as dry stone walling, betting rich buyers will still pay for handmade work.
S3.feel: Anxious with some fight in it, like seeing a storm over the next hill on a long gather.
S3.quote: The part that scares me is watching it come and still not changing, because that's me, I don't change easy.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Emeka's fear shifts from the robots to his own slowness, an unusually honest admission for someone so resistant. Change, for him, has to come through people he trusts, Ruth and Davey, not through information. Buying land is his idea of safety, even in a world of machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. 2036. That's a proper run-up, at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got ten years, so there's no excuse for leaving shepherds and farmhands with nothing at the end. I'd want the union and the government sorting out land and jobs now, not in year nine. That's my public line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years lets me kid myself for about six of them. I'd keep thinking it might not happen, like the hype one. I'd probably still be up the hill in 2034 telling Davey's replacement it'll never come to us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy hill ground if I could, because land would still be land in 2036. I'd keep the flock growing and maybe get to two hundred ewes of my own. I'd stay in the union, and around year five I'd force myself to look at what work is left and do a course then, not before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, oddly. It feels far enough away to breathe, close enough that I know I'm fooling myself a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you'd fool yourself for six years. What would you want someone to say to you in year six?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get off the hill and look, Emeka. That's it, really. Someone I respect, saying it plainly, not some advert.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you want to be in 2036, if you could choose?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On my own bit of hill with my own sheep and a dog that's better than Moss, which is hard to imagine. Maybe the robots do the heavy jobs and I just look after the ground. That's the only good version I can picture.

S4.say: He'd say ten years means there's no excuse for leaving shepherds and farm workers with nothing, and that the union and government should sort out land and jobs now, not at the last minute.
S4.think: He admits ten years would let him pretend for about six that it won't happen, and he can picture himself still on the hill in 2034 saying it won't reach them.
S4.do: Buys hill ground if he can and grows his own flock towards two hundred ewes. Stays in the union and plans to look seriously at other work and take a course around year five.
S4.feel: Calmer, with breathing room, but aware he'd be fooling himself a bit.
S4.quote: Honestly, ten years lets me kid myself for about six of them.
S4.fieldNote: The long run-up lowers his fear but also lowers his urgency, which he names himself. His best future is owning land and looking after it while machines do the heavy work. He wants a plain-spoken person he respects to push him, not a campaign or an advert.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028, no question. There's no time to do anything but get angry. What would help is a proper deal for farm workers before the machines come, like a payout and first refusal on rented land, so people like me can stay on the hill as owners, not just staff.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe who owns the robots. Nobody asked me that and it's the whole thing really. If the farm workers and the small owners owned them together, I'd sleep a lot better.

headlineQuote: Honestly, ten years lets me kid myself for about six of them.
portrait: Emeka Khan is a 27-year-old head shepherd on a hill estate who keeps ninety ewes of his own on rented ground and has never used an AI tool. He trusts land, dogs and people he knows, and he distrusts the estate office far more than any machine. Across the five pictures he reaches for the same answers: the union, fairness for workers, and buying more ground. The faster the change, the angrier and more stuck he feels; with ten years he admits he'd mostly pretend it wasn't coming. His hope is to own a bit of hill and look after it while robots do the heavy work.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because two years leaves him time to get angry but not to change.
whatWouldHelp: A proper deal for farm workers before the machines arrive, such as a payout and first refusal on rented land, and shared ownership of the robots by workers and small owners.
